title: Uncovering spatio-temporal, mechano-transcriptomic signatures of development
text:
Contact PI: Dumitrascu, Bianca
PROJECT NARRATIVE
Tissue morphogenesis is a spatio-temporal process resulting from coordinated changes in gene
expression, cellular morphology and the ability of cells to generate and interpret force. The work
we propose will provide a computational and mathematical language to understand how cells
use gene expression and tension to guide shape changes through directed cellular movements.
Our multi-specie approach will uncover general principles of self-organization which may be
leveraged to design optimal experiments for improving wound healing and regeneration.

title: Expanding the chemical probe development paradigm toward underexplored targets
text:
Although high-throughput screening yields a number of small-molecule modulators of biomedically relevant
proteins, these ‘hits’ typically require substantial optimization to improve their biological functions via costly
medicinal chemistry approaches, creating a significant hurdle to development of efficacious chemical probes and
drugs. The proposed research program aims to address this limitation through two complementary research
directions focused on developing generally applicable medicinal chemistry workflows for underexplored
biological targets. Ultimately, application of these approaches and the resulting probes will advance our
fundamental understanding of living systems and provide proof-of-concept for novel therapeutic mechanisms of
action, thereby enhancing human health.

title: A new humanized mouse model to study HBV gene editing
text:
It is estimated that approximately 300 million people are infected with the hepatitis B virus
(HBV), which is a largely incurable and lifelong infection that is responsible for >800,000 deaths
annually, primarily due to severe symptoms including cirrhosis and liver cancer. Curative
therapies for HBV are desperately needed but the lack of clinically relevant and affordable
animal models for HBV have hindered the development of new therapies. In this proposal we
will use our recently developed and affordable model for HBV to develop and evaluate novel
curative gene therapies that target the HBV virus for elimination in infected cells.

title: Colonoscopy augmentation with Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging (FLIm): colorectal cancer detection in humans
text:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a significant global health burden, and current colonoscopy methods are limited in
detecting subtle structural and biochemical changes in lesions, leading to missed diagnoses. This project aims
to integrate label-free fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIm) into colonoscopy to enhance lesion phenotyping by
providing real-time biochemical information. By creating a comprehensive database of FLIm signatures,
developing advanced analysis algorithms, and evaluating FLIm's diagnostic accuracy, this research seeks to
improve early detection and diagnosis of CRC, ultimately advancing patient care and outcomes.

title: Regulation and mechanisms of sexually dimorphic morphogenesis in C. elegans
text:
Morphogenesis is a universally important process in growth and development that involves changes in cell
shape and position that must occur at precisely the right time and place and sex, yet a comprehensive
understanding is lacking about the cellular mechanisms involved and how they are regulated. In this research
program, we investigate how extrinsic and intrinsic cues are integrated onto the gene regulatory network
(GRN), how the transcriptional regulation by this network is connected to the cellular mechanisms involved in
cellular behaviors of morphogenesis, and how these mechanisms work. This study will lead to a model for how
genes interact to produce biological form, thus providing a basis to identify key components that control
morphogenesis and which could thus provide new targets for pharmaceuticals or other interventions to aid
wound healing or mitigate the effects of morphogenetic faults contributing to birth defects or cancer.

title: Novel EPO peptide therapy for chronic rmTBI dependent neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation
text:
Chronic repeat mild traumatic brain injury (rmTBI) is a neurodegenerative disease with neuroinflammation that
afflicts individuals who have received repeated mild concussions. It appears to be present in a large
percentage of professional players of contact sports and has been found in many studies of military veterans.
Symptoms may include memory and emotional problems, suicidality and dementia. The disease typically
progresses over a period of years or decades, and there is currently no known treatment that can slow or cure
this process. Our laboratory has developed a novel immune regulatory drug (JM4) that shows remarkable
beneficial effects in multiple models of neurodegeneration. We will test the hypothesis that JM4 will
downregulate chronic inflammatory responses and block or reverse the development of rmTBI. We have
recently received FDA approval for use of JM4 as an investigational new drug, and successful findings in this
study may lead rapidly towards development of the first treatment for this devastating disease.

title: Low-dose contrast enhanced fast pediatric brain MRI
text:
Obtaining high quality pediatric brain MRIs with gadolinium (Gd) injection takes long (20+ minutes) time, and
often necessitates sedation or anesthesia, which hinders normal brain development and poses increased risk
for cognitive and behavioral problems later in life. We propose synergistic data acquisition, image
reconstruction and deep learning enhancement strategies that improve pediatric brain imaging by enabling at
most 5-fold reduction in Gd injection dosage and 3-fold acceleration of the typical pediatric brain MRI protocol.
We aim to develop, validate and translate this imaging technology in clinical settings, thus enabling faster and
safer pediatric brain exams with the potential to completely obviate the need for sedation or anesthesia and
significantly reduce the dosage of Gd injections given during an MRI exam.

title: A mechanistic and dyadic approach to identify how interpersonal conscientiousness supports cognitive health and lowers risk of dementia
text:
Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias are a critical public health crisis because there are limited effective
interventions to prevent, slow, or stop disease progression. Conscientiousness is a personality trait that is
associated consistently with lower risk of cognitive impairment, but the mechanisms that explain why
Conscientiousness is protective are not well understood. Identifying the processes through which
Conscientiousness contributes to daily cognition and cognitive decline is critical to develop effective prevention
and intervention strategies to promote healthy cognitive aging.

title: Targeting T Cell Dynamics with IL12mRNA Nanotechnology-Enhanced SBRT to Overcome Immune Suppression in Pancreatic Cancer
text:
Pancreatic cancer remains a lethal malignancy resistant to most therapies, however we have discovered a
preclinical strategy that results in the complete elimination of this difficult-to-treat cancer. The combination of
radiotherapy followed by a mRNA-mediated immunotherapeutic induces a profound immunostimulatory cascade
within the tumor microenvironment, which can now support potent antitumor T cell immunity. This application will
investigate three distinguishing features that drive the unprecedented response we observe against pancreatic
cancer.

title: Regulation of Hepatic Fuel Fluxes by the Mitochondrial Dicarboxylate Carrier
text: The goal of this project is to understand how the mitochondrial dicarboxylate carrier regulates liver gluconeogenic metabolism in normal and type 2 diabetes states. Dysregulated liver metabolism contributes to type 2 diabetes and many other diseases. This project will provide a framework to better understand and potentially treat these diseases.

title: Pathways of Injury and Repair in Barrett's Carcinogenesis
text:
PROGRAM NARRATIVE
Esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is a rapidly rising public health problem and its prognosis remains poor.
Barrett's esophagus (BE) is the precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma but it often goes undetected. The
Program Project focuses on genetic and molecular studies that will develop better understanding of how reflux
injury and repair result in development of BE and its progression to EAC in susceptible individuals. The ultimate
goal is to develop improved methods for detecting BE, predicting its progression to EAC, and preventing BE from
progressing to EAC.

title: Advanced Technology-Core
text: Advanced Technology Core (ATC) As part of the Midwest D-CFAR, the Advanced Technology Core (ATC) will develop, support, and enhance the impact of basic and translational HIV investigators to accelerate progress in priority areas of HIV research and translate research discoveries into improvements in human health. The research enterprise at Washington University (WashU) and Saint Louis University (SLU) is an enormous asset to our growing HIV-investigator community. WashU and SLU received $658.1 million in funding from the National Institutes of Health in 2022. They have a wealth of state-of-the-art core services and a large group of highly trained, highly successful investigators working in disciplines that intersect HIV priority areas, such as microbial pathogenesis, immunology, neuroscience, and inflammatory, metabolic, and cardiovascular diseases. Our outstanding HIV basic and translational scientists are poised for growth, and the ATC will leverage the scientific resources at WashU/SLU and bring together experienced and early-career HIV-focused researchers and non-HIV investigators to drive innovative discovery and translation. The ATC will be led by accomplished basic and translational science investigators and institutional leaders, Drs. Liang Shan and George Kyei. The ATC will contribute to the overall D-CFAR objectives through the establishment of three new units: the Consultation Service Unit (CSU), the Virology Research Unit (VRU), and the Technology Accessibility Unit (TAU). These units will: (1) provide consultation services to foster mentorship and collaborative, multidisciplinary HIV- focused basic research on HIV reservoirs, cure strategy, and HIV-associated comorbidities and coinfections, (2) provide training, reagents, and experimental services for basic and translational HIV research, and (3) provide cost-effective access to state-of-the-art technology in sequencing, imaging, immunophenotyping, and drug discovery. Emerging HIV investigators will be eligible for preferred rates, pilot funds, and microgrants to access cutting-edge technology and ATC services. In addition, we will enhance basic and translational research by providing researchers with access to highly experienced investigators conducting translational research and clinical trials, thereby promoting the development and optimization of novel interventions. Finally, by engaging the sizeable non-HIV-focused research base, the ATC will bring new ideas and approaches to studies focused on HIV cure and HIV-associated comorbidities and coinfections. In summary, the ATC will reduce roadblocks and expand the reach of HIV investigation at WashU and SLU to contribute to the end of the HIV epidemic.

title: InteroCANCEption - Crosstalk Between Cancer and the Central Nervous System
text: Cancer engages the nervous system in ways that can either accelerate malignancy or elicit protective anti-tumor responses, yet the principles governing when nerves act as accomplices versus defenders remain unknown. We propose that this apparent contradiction reflects an unappreciated organizing principle: cancer interoception— the body–brain sensing of tumor state through molecularly defined peripheral sensory circuits and their central integration in the brainstem. We hypothesize that cancer interoception is determined by two key variables: tumor location, which defines the innervation landscape and neuronal subtypes encountered, and cancer genetics, which shapes how tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment engage those neurons. Defining these rules will shift the prevailing cancer-centric paradigm toward a host-oriented framework that enables circuit-level control over tumor progression, immunity, and systemic symptoms. To realize this vision, our team will assist in constructing a cross-cancer Cancer Interoception Roadmap using autochthonous and orthotopic mouse models of lung cancer selected to control tissue macroenvironment and oncogenic genotype. We will generate integrated Cancer Innervation and Cancer Brain Atlases by combining neural tracing and activity mapping with single-cell transcriptomics to identify tumor-engaged peripheral neurons and their central brainstem hubs. We will then establish causality using cell-type-specific neuronal activation, silencing, and ablation to define how distinct neuronal subtypes shape the tumor immune microenvironment, tumor growth, and survival, and to identify key nodes where cancer circuits intersect with metabolic dysfunction and inflammatory states. Finally, we will translate these insights by developing targeted neuromodulation strategies, including druggable neural targets designed to achieve specificity beyond existing systemic neural blockade. Together, this program will establish a generalizable framework to stratify tumors by neural activity and harness body–brain circuits as therapeutic entry points to improve cancer control and patient quality of life.

title: Deciphering Thalamocortical Circuit Dynamics Underlying Pain and Sleep Interactions
text:
NARRATIVE │ Chronic pain affects millions of individuals, and one of its most debilitating consequences is the
disruption of sleep, which exacerbates pain and increases the risk of mental health issues. This R21 project
seeks to uncover the neural mechanisms that link chronic pain and sleep disturbances by investigating
thalamocortical circuits that mediate pain-induced arousal. By using advanced techniques such as closed-loop
optogenetics, in vivo imaging, and deep-learning behavioral tracking, this research aims to identify novel brain
processes as targets to alleviate both pain and its associated sleep disorders, improving overall health outcomes.

title: Core 3: Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core
text: The Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core (Core 3) supports all SPORE Projects by managing, analyzing, and integrating complex, multimodal data sets, including clinical, genomic, imaging and pathology data. Core 3 provides HIPAA-compliant data handling, advanced NGS pipelines, and expert statistical and bioinformatics analysis to ensure rigorous, reproducible, and translational research. It will also develop novel algorithms, guide data sharing and collaborate across Cores to accelerate biomarker discovery and improve lymphoma outcomes.

title: Targeting CD83 to reduce leukemia relapse and GVHD after allogeneichematopoietic cell transplantation
text:
While allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation can cure high risk leukemia, relapse and graft-versus-host
disease (GVHD) account for over 60% of deaths post-transplant. Taking advantage of the differential
expression of CD83 on acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukemia, as well as effector cells of acute and
chronic GVHD, we have developed human CD83-targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells that can
simultaneously protect transplant recipients from relapse and GVHD. In this application, we will test human
CD83-targeted CAR T in eliminating the two major causes of post-transplant mortality using established
xenogeneic models and determine whether CD83 is a therapeutic target and biomarker of acute or chronic
GVHD.

title: Integrating Accelerated Droplet Chemistry with LC-MS for High Throughput Quantitative Analysis
text:
The goal of this research is to create a quantitative mass spectrometry platform for effective analysis of isomeric
species of lipids and saccharides, which are important in metabolism, protein structure, and cell-to-cell signaling.
The novelty of the proposed approach lies in the use of accelerated droplet chemistry to enhance analyte signal
and confer unique fragmentation patterns to differentiate isomers when analyzed in tandem MS. The significance
is that we achieve femtomole level sensitivity by coupling the droplet reaction platform to separation techniques
allowing analysis of <1 µL samples of complex mixtures in a high throughput fashion, a process that is of great
importance in many other fields including combinatorial chemistry.

title: Dissect the consequences of telomere stress on hematopoietic stem cells
text:
The proposed research addresses a fundamental disparity between our comprehensive knowledge of
hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) stress induced by telomere attrition and the lack of strategies for ameliorating
telomere shortening–associated hematological diseases. The successful completion of the proposed aims will
reveal new mechanisms that drive HSC exhaustion and clarify the relationship between telomere damage and
clonal hematopoiesis, thereby providing new opportunities to develop strategies for improving the prevention
and treatment of telomere shortening–related hematological disorders.

title: Quantification of ARIA During the Treatment of Alzheimer's Patients
text:
The purpose of this project is to develop clinical image analysis software which will automatically
detect and quantify the amyloid related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) during the treatment of
Alzheimer’s patients to monitor the effects of the therapeutic intervention, and to improve patient
management. The software will use non-invasive MR images with T1, FLAIR and T2* contrasts
and report the number of lesions, their volume, and their anatomical locations. These tabulated
results, with the images containing highlighted ARIA lesions will help clinicians both to determine
the drug response, and to decide to continue with the drug therapy.

title: Leveraging HSF1 Attenuation to Transform Clonal Hematopoiesis into Beneficial Hematopoiesis
text:
The proposed research aims to redefine the understanding of clonal hematopoiesis by exploring how the
attenuation of HSF1 might potentially redirect detrimental clonal hematopoiesis towards favoring normal
hematopoiesis while inhibiting its progression. These findings hold the potential to significantly impact the
development of targeted interventions, ensuring the preservation of normal hematopoiesis and impeding the
progression of clonal hematopoiesis.
